interest: U.S. moral embargo and public protests against supplying Japan, 1939–41.
overview: This file consists of seventeen consecutive sheets (Sheets 75 through 91) of the Department of State's official 'List of Papers' (docket register) for decimal file 894.24 (Japan: Army Equipment and Supplies), cataloguing sub-numbers 663 through 776 from May 1939 to January 1940. The entries record extensive domestic and international communications regarding the supply of American war materials—most notably scrap iron, steel, aluminum, aeronautical supplies, and aviation gasoline—to Japan during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Alongside voluminous petitions, letters, and legislative inquiries from citizens, peace organizations, religious bodies, and members of Congress urging an embargo on shipments to Japan, the docket documents internal State Department policy deliberations, legal analyses of treaty obligations, and intensive conferences between the Division of Controls and leading American petroleum corporations to enforce a moral embargo against transferring high-octane aviation fuel patents, equipment, and blending agents to Japan and the Soviet Union.

subfiles.about: Official Department of State docket register indexing incoming and outgoing documents, memoranda, and diplomatic communications under decimal file 894.24 (Army Equipment - Japan) for sub-numbers 663 through 776.
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Communications and Records
subfiles.summary: This seventeen-page continuous docket register indexes sub-numbers 663 through 776 in State Department decimal file 894.24, covering records created between May 1939 and January 1940. It chronicles extensive nationwide protests and congressional inquiries concerning American exports of scrap iron, aluminum, aircraft components, and war supplies aiding the Japanese military in China, along with official departmental responses clarifying existing neutrality legislation and treaty commitments. A substantial portion of the register details high-level conferences and confidential exchanges between the Division of Controls and executives of major American petroleum and engineering firms—such as Standard Oil, Shell, Sun Oil, Universal Oil Products, Phillips Petroleum, and Badger & Sons—to institute a voluntary 'moral embargo' prohibiting the transfer of technical data, manufacturing rights, refining equipment, and blending agents for high-octane aviation fuel to Japan and the Soviet Union.
